To achieve this, the character must move to an adjacent intact cell (if any) and then move back onto the start cell (now still cracked) to fall. This requires at least one adjacent intact cell. If no adjacent intact cell exists (or all neighbors are out of bounds), it's impossible.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting to handle start=end case separately, or incorrectly always returning YES/NO.

special_cases.description: Destination is initially intact ('.'). To fall through it, the character must step onto it twice: first to crack it, then later to fall. This requires a path that can reach the destination from an adjacent cell, then leave to an adjacent intact cell, then step back onto the destination. Essentially, there must be at least one adjacent intact cell to the destination that is reachable from the first visit, and the overall path must allow this double visit without stepping on other cracked cells.
special_cases.test_values: Grid where destination is '.' and all its neighbors are 'X' or out of bounds -> NO. Grid where destination has at least one neighbor '.' and there is a path start->neighbor->destination->neighbor->destination -> YES.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming one visit to destination is enough, or not considering the need for a second visit after cracking.

special_cases.description: Destination is initially cracked ('X'). The character only needs to step onto it once to fall. special_cases.expected_behavior: Return YES if there is a path of '.' cells from start to a neighbor of destination, else NO.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Treating destination as a normal cell that cannot be stepped onto because it's cracked, or not allowing the final step onto a cracked cell.

Handle special case when start == end
Distinguish between destination being initially intact vs cracked
common_pitfalls: Incorrectly allowing traversal over cracked cells (other than destination) leading to false positives
Not handling start==end case
Assuming the destination can be stepped onto only once
Using BFS without considering that ice state changes, leading to incorrect visited marking

implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Mathematical property of permutation square roots: a cycle of length L in p corresponds to a cycle of length L in q if L is odd, or to two cycles of length L/2 in q if L is even, requiring pairing.

implicit_constraints.description: Algorithm must handle up to n=10^6 efficiently, requiring O(n) or O(n log n) time and O(n) memory.
The input permutation p may contain cycles that need to be processed; use iterative approach to avoid recursion depth issues.

special_cases.test_values: n=4, p=[2,1,3,4] - one 2-cycle and two fixed points
special_cases.common_mistakes: Failing to check pairing of even cycles; attempting to construct q from unpaired even cycle

special_cases.description: Solution with multiple cycles
special_cases.common_mistakes: Incorrectly merging cycles; producing invalid q that doesn't square to p

special_cases.description: Large odd cycle
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output a q that is also a 5-cycle (e.g., [4,5,1,2,3])
special_cases.common_mistakes: Treating odd cycle as even; incorrect construction

problem_type_analysis.sub_category: permutation square root via cycle decomposition
key_operations: handle odd-length cycles: construct q cycle of same length by placing element at index i to position i+ (len+1)/2? Actually standard: For odd length L, q^2 = cycle of length L means q is also a cycle of length L, where q[i] = p^{(L+1)/2}(i). Essentially, we need to map each element to its image under the square root. Common method: For odd cycle (a1 a2 ... aL), q is (a1 a_{(L+3)/2} a2 a_{(L+5)/2} ... )
handle even-length cycles by pairing two cycles of same length and constructing a q cycle of double length
common_pitfalls: Forgetting that even cycles must be paired
Incorrectly constructing q from odd cycles (off-by-one errors)
Using recursion for cycle extraction causing stack overflow
Not resetting visited array correctly for large n

input_format.description: First line: two integers n and m. Second line: n integers a_i.

output_format.description: First line: two integers l and kmax (l <= m, kmax is length of optimal subsequence). Second line: kmax integers (positions in ascending order).

implicit_constraints.description: Only elements <= m can be part of a subsequence with LCM <= m, because any element > m in the subsequence would make the LCM at least that element > m.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: definition of LCM and constraint l <= m

implicit_constraints.description: The LCM of a subsequence must be a multiple of each element; hence each element must divide the LCM. Therefore, for a given l, only elements that divide l can be included.

The answer l can be any integer from 1 to m, but the longest subsequence will consist of all elements that are divisors of l, because including any additional divisor of l does not increase LCM beyond l (since all divide l). The LCM of all divisors of l is exactly l if the set includes enough prime powers, but even if not, it is still a divisor of l and thus ≤ l.
The solution can use a frequency array of size m+1 and a divisor-counting sieve (update multiples) to count how many elements divide each value.

special_cases.description: All elements > m. Then no element can be used except empty subsequence. Output l=1, kmax=0, and no positions line (or an empty line).
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output: 1 0 (then no second line or empty line depending on format; typically no second line printed when kmax=0).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting to handle empty subsequence; printing a second line with 0 positions or crashing.

special_cases.description: m = 1. Only elements equal to 1 can be used. The subsequence can include all 1's. The LCM of any set of 1's is 1 ≤ 1, so optimal subsequence includes all 1's. Output l=1 and kmax = count of 1's.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Including element 2 or 3 if they are ≤ m? Here m=1, so only 1 is usable. Mistake: not filtering out elements > m.

special_cases.description: All elements are 1. Then any l from 1 to m works, but the longest subsequence includes all elements since LCM of all 1's is 1 ≤ m. So output l=1, kmax=n.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Choosing a larger l like 2 or 3 might still have all 1's but l is not necessarily the LCM; but any l ≤ m is allowed. However, the algorithm typically picks the l with maximum count; since only 1's exist, count for l=1 is n; for other l, if 1 divides l, count also n. So multiple correct outputs.

special_cases.description: Elements include prime numbers and composites. The optimal l might be a composite number that many divisors share.
special_cases.expected_behavior: The longest subsequence: for l=6 (or l=2,3,10 etc?). Count divisors of 2: all 2's (3 elements), divisors of 3: all 3's (3 elements), divisors of 6: all 2's and 3's (6 elements) because 2 and 3 divide 6. So l=6 gives 6 elements, which is maximum. Output l=6, kmax=6, positions of all 6 elements.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not considering that composite l can include elements from different primes; only counting divisors of individual primes.

key_operations: Frequency counting of elements up to m
For each value d from 1 to m, add its frequency to all multiples of d (sieve-like update)
Find the value with maximum total count
Output the value and the original positions of elements that divide that value
common_pitfalls: Ignoring elements > m (they can't be used)
Using map or slow data structures instead of array for frequencies (since m ≤ 1e6)
Not handling the empty subsequence case when no element divides any l (or when l=1 is considered separately)
Outputting indices in incorrect order (must be ascending)
Forgetting that the LCM of the chosen subsequence might be less than the selected l, but that's fine as long as it's ≤ m
Integer overflow when counting frequencies (use int, n ≤ 1e6 so int is fine; but sum of frequencies could be n ≤ 1e6, still fine)
Time complexity: naive O(m sqrt(m)) may TLE; must use sieve-like O(m log m) or O(m log log m)

Wait, need to recalc: Actually using correct forward simulation: start 7, first halfplus: pays for floor(7/2)=3 apples (30), takes 4 apples, left 3. Second halfplus: pays for floor(3/2)=1 apple (10), takes 2 apples, left 1. Third halfplus: pays for floor(1/2)=0 (0), takes 1 apple, left 0. Total 40. But example output is 55. So my forward simulation is wrong. The correct forward simulation: For halfplus, they pay for the number of apples they buy? Actually they buy exactly half of the apples. input_format.description: First line contains two integers n and m. Then n lines each contain an integer k_i (1 or 2) followed by k_i integers a_{i,j} representing literals (positive for variable, negative for negation).

fields.name: clauses
fields.dimension: each clause: k_i followed by k_i integers

output_format.description: Print a single integer — the number of assignments satisfying the equation, modulo 1e9+7.

explicit.description: Literal: positive for variable, negative for negation, absolute value ≤ m, non-zero
Each variable appears at most twice in total (including negation) across all clauses

implicit_constraints.description: The formula is a XOR of clauses, each clause is an OR of at most two literals. Due to variable occurrence ≤2, the graph where variables are nodes and clauses are edges (with polarity) forms a collection of paths and cycles (including self-loops and multiple edges?).
Clauses of size 1 are simply literals. Clauses of size 2 may have both literals being the same variable, leading to that variable itself (x OR x = x) or (¬x OR ¬x = ¬x).
Clauses with both x and ¬x are always true, so they do not impose any constraint.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: clause contains a variable and its negation

boundary_conditions.condition: min and max number of clauses
min and max number of variables

special_cases.description: Variable appears twice in the same clause (e.g., '2 1 1' or '2 -3 -3')
special_cases.expected_behavior: The clause reduces to the literal itself, not a pair. Counting should treat it as a single literal clause.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Treating it as a proper OR of two distinct variables, leading to incorrect equation outcomes.

special_cases.description: Clause contains both x and ¬x (e.g., '2 1 -1')
special_cases.expected_behavior: This clause is always true (tautology), so it imposes no constraint. The number of satisfying assignments is 2^m.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Treating it as a constraint that can be satisfied by some assignments but not others; actually it's always satisfied.

special_cases.description: Variable appears zero times in the formula
special_cases.test_values: n=0? but n≥1, so m>n with some variables unused
special_cases.expected_behavior: Such variables are free, contributing a factor of 2 each.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting to account for free variables in counting.

special_cases.description: Components with cycles (variables appearing twice forming a cycle)
special_cases.test_values: Multiple clauses forming a cycle of variables, e.g., clauses: (x1 OR x2), (x2 OR x3), (x3 OR x1) – but limited to occurrence ≤2, so cycle possible if each appears twice? Actually with each variable at most twice, cycles of length >2 require each variable appears exactly twice? Could be possible.
special_cases.expected_behavior: The DP must handle cycles correctly, possibly using linear equations on parity.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming tree structure only, missing cycles.

problem_type_analysis.sub_category: Counting assignments on paths and cycles with XOR of ORs
key_operations: Build graph from clauses where each variable is a node and each clause is an edge labeled with polarities
Handle clauses of size 1 (unit clauses) separately
Perform DP on each connected component (paths and cycles) to count valid assignments
Combine results from components and free variables using multiplication modulo 1e9+7
common_pitfalls: Not handling duplicate literals in a clause correctly
Forgetting that clauses with both variable and its negation are tautologies
Incorrect modulo operations
Overlooking free variables that do not appear in any clause
Mishandling negation literals in graph representation (polarity matters)

special_cases.expected_behavior: Must shift the last character (or any character, but lexicographically smallest is to shift the rightmost 'a', i.e., last character). Output is (n-1) 'a's followed by 'z'.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Shifting the first character instead, producing 'za...a' which is lexicographically larger

special_cases.description: String contains no 'a' characters
special_cases.expected_behavior: Shift the entire string (or all consecutive non-'a' from first character) to achieve maximum decrease.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Stopping early or shifting only part of the non-'a' run, resulting in a larger string

special_cases.description: Multiple groups of non-'a' separated by 'a's
special_cases.expected_behavior: Only the first group of consecutive non-'a' starting from the first non-'a' should be shifted.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Shifting across 'a's, or shifting a later group

special_cases.expected_behavior: Shift the only character. For 'a', output is 'z'. For 'b', output is 'a'.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting that 'a' becomes 'z'

common_pitfalls: Not handling all 'a's case
Shifting beyond the first non-'a' run
Off-by-one errors in substring indices

input_format.description: Two lines, each containing a day of the week (lowercase English string from the set: monday, tuesday, wednesday, thursday, friday, saturday, sunday).

output_format.description: Print YES if there exists a non-leap year and a pair of consecutive months such that the first day of the first month is the given first day and the first day of the next month is the given second day, otherwise print NO.

implicit_constraints.description: The input strings are always from the set of seven day names.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: 'It's guaranteed that each string in the input is from the set ...'

implicit_constraints.description: The year considered is a non-leap year, so February has 28 days.
The first day of each month in a non-leap year is determined by the day of the week of January 1. The day of the week advances by the number of days in the previous month modulo 7.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement implicitly requires checking all pairs of consecutive months.

special_cases.description: Same day for both months: e.g., sunday sunday.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output YES because there exists a pair of consecutive months with same first day (e.g., February and March in 2015).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming that consecutive months always have different first days due to varying month lengths; but some month pairs have length multiple of 7 (e.g., February has 28 days, which is exactly 4 weeks).

special_cases.description: Difference of 1 day: e.g., monday tuesday.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output NO because no consecutive months have a difference of 1 day (since month lengths are 28, 29, 30, 31; modulo 7, the possible differences are 0, 2, 3, 5).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Thinking that any consecutive days can appear; but the only possible differences between first days of consecutive months are those that correspond to the number of days in the first month modulo 7.

special_cases.description: Difference of 2 days: e.g., saturday tuesday.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output YES because there is a month with 31 days following a month with 30 days? Actually difference: from Saturday to Tuesday is +3 days, but example says YES. Check note: July 1 Saturday, August 1 Tuesday (July has 31 days, which is 31 mod 7 = 3, so +3 days). So difference of 3 days is possible.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Confusing the direction: the second day must be exactly the first day of the next month.

key_operations: Computing possible differences (days in month mod 7)
Checking if given difference exists among month lengths
common_pitfalls: Assuming all differences are possible
Forgetting that February has 28 days in non-leap year

Not considering both orders of months (first month then next) because the problem specifies first day of some month and first day of the next month; the first given day is the first month, second given day is the next month.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Overcomplicating; DP should handle base case.

special_cases.description: T is very large, allowing a long path. The solution should find the longest path (by number of nodes) from 1 to n that does not exceed T. Since T is large, the longest topological path may be taken.
special_cases.test_values: n=5, m=4, T=1e9, edges: 1->2, 2->3, 3->4, 4->5 with small times.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming T restricts path length too much; need to handle large T.

special_cases.test_values: n=4, m=3, T=13, edges: 1->2 (5), 2->3 (7), 2->4 (8). Path 1-2-4 has time 13 and 3 nodes; path 1-2-3-4 not possible.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not considering that time to reach a node depends on how many nodes visited; need DP over nodes visited.

special_cases.description: Graph may have nodes not reachable from 1 or not reaching n, but guaranteed path exists. DP must ignore unreachable states.
special_cases.test_values: n=3, m=2, edges: 1->2 (1), 2->3 (1), but no direct edge; T=2.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Initializing all states with large or infinite time; need to start from node 1 with dp[1][1]=0.

problem_type_analysis.sub_category: DP on DAG with state (node, count) minimizing cost
key_operations: DP transition: for edge (u,v,t) and count k: dp[v][k+1] = min(dp[v][k+1], dp[u][k] + t)
Reconstruction of path by storing predecessor
Iterate over k from 1 to n to find largest k where dp[n][k] <= T
common_pitfalls: Using time as DP dimension (too large)
Not handling large sums (use long long)
Forgetting that the path must start at 1 and end at n; DP for other nodes irrelevant
Incorrect reconstruction due to multiple predecessors

But any edge on the path is a bridge because only one path. So answer should be min weight among edges on any s-t path? Actually since all paths share common edges? Here there is only one path. special_cases.test_values: n=3, edges: 1-2 cost 1, 1-3 cost 1e9, 2-3 cost 1e9, s=1, t=3. The only s-t paths: 1-2-3 (cost 1+1e9) and 1-3 direct (cost 1e9). There is a bridge? Edge 1-3 is not a bridge because there is alternative path 1-2-3. So need to break both? Actually to disconnect s and t, we can remove edge 1-3, but then still path 1-2-3 exists. So need to remove either edge 1-2 and edge 1-3? That would break all paths: remove 1-2 and 1-3 leaves no connection. So cost 1+1e9. Or remove 1-2 and 2-3? cost 1+1e9. Or remove 1-3 and 2-3? cost 2e9. So optimal is remove 1-2 and 1-3? Wait, but edge 1-2 cost 1, edge 1-3 cost 1e9, total 1e9+1. But we could also remove the bridge? Actually edge 1-2 is a bridge? In graph, edge 1-2: if removed, still 1-3 and 3-2. So not bridge. So we need two edges. Which two? Any pair that intersects all paths. The minimal is pair (1-2, 1-3) cost 1+1e9, or (1-2, 2-3) cost 1+1e9, or (1-3, 2-3) cost 2e9. So answer should be 1e9+1. But note that removing just edge 1-2 (cost 1) does not disconnect because path 1-3-2 exists; removing just edge 1-3 (cost 1e9) leaves path 1-2-3. So two edges needed.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming a single bridge exists.

Assuming that s and t are initially connected
Incorrect handling of case where zero roads needed
Not considering that removing a road may open new paths? No, removal only breaks.
Overlooking parallel edges when checking if a single edge removal disconnects s and t

input_format.description: A single line containing a string s of 27 uppercase English letters, each letter appears at least once.

output_format.description: Two lines each consisting of 13 uppercase English characters representing the rows of the grid, or 'Impossible' if no solution exists.

implicit_constraints.description: The grid has exactly 2 rows and 13 columns, so 26 tiles.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: 'grid to be a set of tiles with 2 rows and 13 columns'

implicit_constraints.description: Each of the 26 letters appears exactly once in the grid (since s has 27 letters, one letter appears twice, so the path must revisit a tile).
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Input: s length 27 with each letter at least once, grid has 26 cells.

implicit_constraints.description: The path can use a tile multiple times, but cannot occupy two consecutive places (since no tile is adjacent to itself).
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: 'A single tile can be used more than once by a path (though the tile cannot occupy two consecutive places)'

implicit_constraints.description: Adjacency includes diagonal neighbors, so each tile has up to 8 neighbors (except borders).
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: 'two tiles are adjacent if they share a side or a corner'

implicit_constraints.description: The path must traverse the grid in the order given by s.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: 'Find a grid that contains a path whose tiles... form the string s'

special_cases.description: The duplicate letter appears at two positions that are adjacent in the path (consecutive reuse is not allowed).
special_cases.test_values: Any string where the repeated letter's occurrences are consecutive in s
special_cases.expected_behavior: The solution must avoid placing the two occurrences in the same tile consecutively; if forced, it's impossible.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming consecutive reuse is allowed or not checking adjacency properly.

special_cases.description: The path may need to start or end at a border tile to allow proper traversal of all letters.
special_cases.test_values: Strings where the first and last letters are far apart in the grid
special_cases.expected_behavior: The construction algorithm should consider starting positions carefully.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Starting at an interior tile that restricts movement.

key_operations: Determine positions of each letter in the grid
Construct grid layout to satisfy path adjacency
Handle the duplicate letter by revisiting a tile
common_pitfalls: Not considering diagonal adjacency, resulting in invalid paths
Assuming the path is simple (no revisits) when it must revisit exactly one tile
Failing to account for reduced adjacency at borders
Incorrectly handling the duplicate letter's two occurrences

output_format.description: For each type 1 event, output a line containing integer t followed by t integers (girl indices) in order from best to worst.

implicit_constraints.triggered_by: problem statement: 'We will consider the NYC as a rooted tree with root being junction 1.'

implicit_constraints.description: Girls' initial weights equal their index i, which is between 1 and m. So weights are distinct at start? Actually indices are unique, weight equals index, so weights are distinct. But after updates, weights can become equal due to increments; ordering tie-breaking uses junction index.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: definition of 'better' and initial weights = i.

implicit_constraints.description: Each girl can be invited at most once. Once invited, they are removed from consideration.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: 'best girls he still have not invited' and examples.

special_cases.expected_behavior: Output line with 0 and no additional integers.

special_cases.test_values: v with no c_i in its subtree.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Still performing update operation unnecessarily.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Output more than available or crash.

special_cases.description: Many type 2 updates on same subtree causing large weights.
special_cases.test_values: Repeated updates on subtree of root.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Integer overflow.

special_cases.test_values: v = u = some node with girls.

ordering by weight then by junction index

Ensuring correct tie-breaking when weights equal
Efficiently finding k smallest on path without iterating all
Subtree updates affect many girls, need lazy or segment tree with DFS order

input_format.description: First line: two integers n and c. Then n lines, each starting with integer l_i followed by l_i integers representing the word.

fields.name: words
fields.dimension: each word is a list of l_i integers

output_format.description: A single integer x (0 <= x <= c-1) representing the required number of rotations, or -1 if impossible.

implicit_constraints.description: The total length constraint (<= 1e6) prohibits algorithms with time complexity O(n * c) or O(total * c). Must be near linear in total length and c.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: total length <= 1e6 and c up to 1e6

implicit_constraints.description: When c = 1, all hieroglyphs are 1, and the shift is identity for any x (only x=0 possible). The sequence is always sorted if all words consist of 1s (which they do). Output 0.

boundary_conditions.condition: minimum and maximum total length (min is n)

special_cases.description: All words are identical. After any rotation, they remain identical, so sequence is sorted. The answer can be 0 or any x (0..c-1) but we output 0 for simplicity.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming only x=0 works, but any x is valid; however, since problem says print any, 0 is fine.

special_cases.description: Sequence is already sorted without any rotation (x=0 works).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Thinking that rotation is always needed.

special_cases.description: Two words where the first is a prefix of the second and all characters in the prefix are equal. After any rotation, the relative order of equal characters remains unchanged, so the shorter word must come first. If the first word is longer, it will always be greater, making it impossible to sort.
special_cases.test_values: n=2, c=5, words: [3,1,2,3], [2,1,2] (first is longer and matches prefix of second)
special_cases.common_mistakes: Trying to shift to make the longer word smaller, but shifting does not affect length.

special_cases.description: When the first differing characters can be made equal by a shift? Actually shift adds same amount to both, so the difference in value remains the same modulo c. So the condition for sorting at first difference is: (a_i + x) mod c < (b_i + x) mod c in cyclic order. This imposes intervals on x.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Correctly compute intervals and find intersection
special_cases.common_mistakes: Off-by-one errors due to wrap-around (c->1) and handling of mod.

key_operations: For each adjacent pair, compute the allowed x intervals that make the pair sorted
Intersect all intervals to find a common x
Handle prefix case where no difference exists
common_pitfalls: Mishandling the wrap-around when characters are equal modulo c
Forgetting that shift does not change lexicographic order when words are identical up to the shorter length
Assuming intervals are always contiguous; they may be two intervals due to wrap
Not considering the case where c is small and intervals may be empty

input_format.description: First line contains four integers x0, y0, v, T. Second line contains integer n. Then n lines each contain three integers xi, yi, ri.

output_format.description: Single real number representing the probability that the cockroach survives.

implicit_constraints.description: The cockroach's initial position may lie inside a shadow circle; in that case it is already safe and probability = 1.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Definition of survival: cockroach stops if at time t<=T it reaches any shadow circle. At t=0 it is already in shadow if inside a circle.

implicit_constraints.description: The probability is the fraction of the full 360-degree range of directions that lead to survival, bounded by [0,1].
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Definition of probability as uniform random direction.

implicit_constraints.description: Coordinates and distances can be up to order 1e9, and v*T up to 1e18, requiring careful handling of floating point precision and avoiding overflow in intermediate calculations.

special_cases.description: v=0 or T=0: cockroach does not move or has no time. Survival only if it starts inside a shadow circle.
special_cases.test_values: x0=0,y0=0,v=0,T=1,n=1,circle: 1 0 1 -> outside so probability 0; or v=1,T=0 with same -> probability 0. If start inside: x0=0,y0=0,circle: 0 0 1, then probability 1.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Handle distance-based computation correctly: if R=0, only circles that contain the start point yield survival.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting to check if start is inside a circle when v*T is 0.

special_cases.description: Start point lies inside a shadow circle: probability = 1 regardless of other parameters.
special_cases.test_values: x0=0,y0=0,v=1,T=10,n=1,circle: 0 0 5 (center at origin, radius 5). Start inside.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not checking inside condition early, leading to incorrect angular computations or double counting.

special_cases.description: A shadow circle completely encloses the reachable region (v*T large): probability = 1 if the entire angular range is covered.
special_cases.test_values: x0=0,y0=0,v=100,T=100,n=1,circle: 0 0 1000. The circle covers all directions within distance 10000, so all directions survive.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Merge the single interval covering [0,2π) and output 1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not handling the case where intervals wrap around and cover the full circle; should sum angles and compare to 2π.

special_cases.description: Multiple circles overlapping: the union of angular intervals may have gaps; need to merge correctly.
special_cases.test_values: x0=0,y0=0,v=1,T=1,n=2, circles: (1,0,1) and (-1,0,1). They cover angles near 0° and 180°, giving two intervals. Probability = (angle sum)/2π.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Compute each interval, sort by start, merge, sum lengths.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not handling cyclic intervals; not accounting for intervals that cross 0°.

key_operations: Compute angular interval for each circle that can be reached within distance v*T
Merge overlapping intervals to get total covered angle
common_pitfalls: Precision errors when using acos or atan2
Integer overflow when computing squared distances
Not handling the case when the start point is inside a circle
Not properly handling intervals that cover the entire 2π range

simulate match creation by repeatedly reducing highest ratings

input_format.description: A single line containing three integers b, d, and s.

output_format.description: A single integer representing the minimum possible number of missed meals.

Actually on same row, Rook attacks along row, so that's attack; but if Bishop is same diagonal? Let's adjust: King at (0,0), Bishop at (1,1) (diagonal), Rook at (2,2) (diagonal). The Bishop can attack, so king in check. But if Bishop is at (1,1) and Rook at (2,2), Bishop is closer and can attack, so check. To test blocking: King at (0,0), Rook at (1,0), another Rook at (2,0). The closest rook can attack, so check. Need case where closest cannot attack but farther can. Example: King at (0,0), Bishop at (1,0) (orthogonal but not diagonal), Bishop cannot attack along orthogonal; Rook at (2,0) (orthogonal), Rook can attack. But Bishop is closer? Actually Bishop is at (1,0) on same row, but Bishop cannot attack horizontally, so it does not block? Wait, blocking: any piece blocks the path, even if it cannot attack. So the farther piece cannot attack due to blocking. So to have a farther piece attack, the closer piece must not block? Actually any piece blocks regardless of type. So actually, the closest piece in each direction determines if king is in check, because any piece farther is blocked by the closest one. So special case: if the closest piece in a direction cannot attack, then king is not in check from that direction. That's standard. m equals number of distinct values of f, which must be fixed points of f, and m ≤ n because h is injective.
For any x, f(x) is a fixed point of f.

special_cases.description: Constant function with f(x)=k for all x; works iff f(k)=k.
special_cases.test_values: n=3, f=[2,2,2] (works if k=2 is fixed; actually 2 is in [1,3], but f(2)=2, so works)
special_cases.common_mistakes: assuming any constant works without checking f(k)=k

special_cases.description: Permutation that is not identity, e.g., 2-cycle.
special_cases.common_mistakes: trying to construct g,h despite condition violation

special_cases.description: Already a function with all fixed points, e.g., identity.
special_cases.common_mistakes: none

common_pitfalls: forgetting to check f(f(x)) == f(x)
incorrectly assigning indices when values repeat
output order of h must match indices used in g

input_format.description: The first line contains two integers n and k. The second line contains n integers t_i.

output_format.description: Print a single integer - the minimum number of tire changes, or -1 if impossible.

explicit.description: maximum number of days winter tires can be used, not exceeding n
average air temperature on day i

implicit_constraints.description: If the number of negative days exceeds k, it is impossible to drive safely throughout winter.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Each negative day requires winter tires, and winter tires are limited to k days.

implicit_constraints.description: If there are no negative days, Vasya can drive using summer tires every day, resulting in zero tire changes.
The car starts with summer tires, so the first switch to winter tires counts as one change.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: before the first winter day Vasya uses summer tires.

implicit_constraints.description: Winter tires can be used on non-negative days, but it consumes the limited k days.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Winter tires can be used at any temperature.

implicit_constraints.description: If the last segment of winter tires ends on day n, no switch back to summer is needed, saving one change.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: At the end of winter, car can be with any set of tires.

implicit_constraints.description: The optimal strategy merges the smallest gaps between negative segments first to minimize the number of segments.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Greedy approach: using spare winter days to cover gaps reduces the number of segments, each saving two changes.

boundary_conditions.condition: minimum and maximum number of days

special_cases.description: No negative days: all t_i >= 0.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting to handle this case, resulting in output -1 or wrong number.

special_cases.description: Number of negative days equals k exactly, no spare.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output 4 (two separate negative segments, each requiring a switch on and off, total 4 changes).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Incorrectly counting changes without considering segments.

special_cases.description: Last segment ends at day n, saving one change.
special_cases.test_values: n=3, k=3, t=[-1,-2,-3] (all negative, last day is n)
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output 1 (switch to winter on day 1, no switch back).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Outputting 2 (counting an unnecessary switch back).

special_cases.description: Using spare days to extend the last segment to the end.
special_cases.test_values: n=5, k=3, t=[-5,0,0,-3,0] (negatives at days 1 and 4; spare=1; gaps=2 between groups; tail=1 after last negative). Without tail extension: groups=2, changes=4, spare=1, gap=2 not enough, so output 4. With tail extension: spare can cover tail, reduces changes to 3.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not considering tail extension, resulting in output 4 instead of 3.

key_operations: Use spare days greedily to merge groups
Extend last segment to end if possible
common_pitfalls: Overcounting changes when the last segment ends at n
Not handling the case of no negative days
Forgetting to consider extending the last segment to the end
Incorrectly computing spare days or gap lengths

input_format.description: First line contains n, the number of vertices. Then n-1 lines each contain two integers u and v describing an edge.

output_format.description: Print a single integer: the minimum number of edges in a possible path after folding, or -1 if impossible.

implicit_constraints.description: The tree is connected and acyclic (given).
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: 'It is guaranteed that the given graph is a tree.'

implicit_constraints.description: Operation requires two disjoint paths of equal length from a vertex v, and all internal vertices of the paths must have degree exactly 2 (no other neighbors).
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Description of the operation: 'vertices a1,...,ak,b1,...,bk must not have any neighbours in the tree other than adjacent vertices of corresponding paths.'

implicit_constraints.description: After merging, the tree becomes smaller; the process can be repeated. The final result must be a path.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Goal: 'make the tree into a path via a sequence of described operations'

special_cases.description: Tree is already a path (line tree). The solution must handle this case; path can be further reduced if there exists a vertex with two equal-length branches (e.g., the middle vertex of an odd-length path). After folding, the minimal path length may be 1.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output 1 (since path can be folded to a single edge).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming no operation is needed and outputting original length (2).

special_cases.description: Tree is a star (one center with many leaves). The center has multiple pendant vertices, each forming a path of length 1. The operation can merge pairs of leaves repeatedly until one remains, resulting in a path of length 1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting that internal vertices (leaves) have no other neighbors, so condition holds.

special_cases.description: Tree with a node having two branches of different lengths, making folding impossible. For example, a simple 'T' shape where one branch is longer than the other.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output -1 (since no vertex has two equal-length clean paths).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Attempting to fold anyway or not detecting impossibility.

key_operations: DFS to compute depths and subtree sizes
Dynamic programming to determine if a subtree can be folded and to what length
Merging equal-length branches from a node
Finding the shortest possible path after folding
common_pitfalls: Not updating the tree structure after a merge (which can affect further operations)
Incorrectly handling that internal vertices of paths must have degree exactly 2 (no extra branches)
Assuming that if the tree can be folded, the final path length is determined solely by some parity or diameter
Forgetting that the operation requires paths to be disjoint except at the root

implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Description of mouse behavior and the goal to compute minimal hungry mice.

implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Description: moving speeds equal; those that reach first eat.

special_cases.description: No cheese pieces (M=0). All mice remain hungry.

input_format.description: First line: three integers n, m, d. Next n lines: each contains two integers ci, wi (Physics cup). Next m lines: each contains two integers cj, wj (Informatics cup).

output_format.description: Print a single integer: the maximum possible total significance, or 0 if no valid selection.

implicit_constraints.description: Cups of each subject must be sorted by significance descending; the set of chosen cups from each subject must be a prefix of this sorted list (i.e., if a cup is chosen, all cups with higher significance for that subject must also be chosen).
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Rule: if a cup for a subject with significance x is exposed, then all cups for this subject with significance greater than x must be exposed too.

implicit_constraints.description: The problem requires selecting at least one cup from each subject, so the most significant cup of each subject must be included if any cup from that subject is included. Therefore, the total width of the most significant cups from both subjects must not exceed d; otherwise answer is 0.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Constraint 'there is at least one Physics cup and at least one Informatics cup' combined with prefix rule.

special_cases.description: The most significant cup of Physics has width greater than d, making it impossible to include any Physics cup (since it must be included if any Physics cup is included). Similarly for Informatics. If both top cups' widths exceed d individually, no solution; also if sum of top widths > d, then no solution.
special_cases.test_values: n=1,m=1, d=1, Physics cup: (10, 5), Informatics cup: (10, 5) -> sum=10>1 => output 0
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output 0 because minimal total width exceeds d.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming you can omit the top cup, or forgetting to check the top cup width alone.

special_cases.description: Large n,m up to 100k, so O(n log n) or O(n log m) is needed; O(n*m) will TLE.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Algorithm should run within time limits (typically 2 sec).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Using naive O(n*m) approach.

special_cases.description: All cups have very large widths, so only a few cups can fit. The prefix constraint may force inclusion of high-significance but large-width cups, possibly limiting the selection.
special_cases.test_values: d small, so only very narrow cups can be selected; need to consider trade-offs
special_cases.expected_behavior: Correctly compute maximum total significance under width constraint.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not considering that including a high-significance cup may force many large-width cups.

key_operations: sort by significance descending for both lists
compute prefix sums of significance and width
iterate over one prefix and use two-pointer/binary search on the other to satisfy width constraint
common_pitfalls: forgetting to sort by significance
not handling the at-least-one constraint correctly
overflow in sum (up to 1e5 * 1e9 = 1e14, use 64-bit)
not considering the case where the most significant cup alone exceeds d

input_format.description: First line contains three integers n, m, k. Then m lines, each containing two integers u, v representing a road between cities u and v.

output_format.description: Print a single integer, the minimum number of additional roads needed.

implicit_constraints.description: The graph is undirected, no self-loops, and at most one edge between any pair of cities.
The initial provinces are the connected components of the road graph. After building additional roads, provinces become the connected components of the updated road graph.

Each city can be incident to at most one tunnel, and each province can have at most k tunnels incident to its cities. Therefore, the number of tunnels that can be attached to a province of size s is min(k, s).

To connect all provinces into one component using tunnels alone (without roads), we need a spanning tree of the province graph, requiring r-1 tunnels if there are r provinces. Each tunnel uses one capacity from each of the two provinces it connects, so total capacity needed is 2*(r-1). Thus, if total capacity (sum of min(k, s_i) over provinces) is at least 2*(r-1), zero roads are needed.

If total capacity is insufficient, we need to merge provinces via roads. Each road reduces the number of provinces by 1 and changes capacities (the new province capacity is min(k, sum of sizes of merged provinces). To minimize roads, we should merge provinces with smallest sizes first, as this minimizes capacity loss.
The input size up to 1e6 requires an O(n log n) or O(n) algorithm.

boundary_conditions.condition: all cities isolated (m=0) and k=1 => output max(0, n-2)
all cities isolated and k >= n => output max(0, n - (n+2)/2)? Actually 0 if n <= 2

special_cases.description: All cities are isolated (no roads). Then each component size 1, capacity min(k,1)=1 for k>=1. Number of components r=n. Need to check if total capacity n >= 2(n-1) => n <= 2. If n>2, need roads. The minimal number of roads is the smallest number of merges to reduce r such that condition holds.
special_cases.test_values: n=3, m=0, k=1 => output 1; n=4, m=0, k=1 => output 2; n=5, m=0, k=2 => capacities all 1? Actually k=2, size 1 gives capacity 1, so same as k=1; output? Let's compute: n=5, r=5, sum=5, need 8 capacities, insufficient. Merge two: new component size2 capacity min(2,2)=2, capacities now [2,1,1,1] sum=5, r=4, need 6 capacities, still insufficient. Merge another two: [2,2,1] sum=5, r=3, need 4 capacities, sum=5>=4, ok. So 2 roads. So answer 2.
special_cases.expected_behavior: The algorithm should compute component sizes, sort them, and greedily merge smallest until capacity condition met.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming that merging always increases capacity; not considering that capacity is capped at k; off-by-one on the number of tunnels required.

special_cases.description: Large component with size > k. Its capacity is k, not size. If multiple such components exist, they each provide only k capacity. This may force more roads.
special_cases.test_values: n=10, m=0, k=3. All isolated? Actually if all isolated, sizes 1, capacities 1 each, sum=10, r=10, need 18 capacities, insufficient. But if there is one component of size 10, capacity 3, r=1 already, so 0 roads. So focus on case where some components are large.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Component capacity is min(k,size). So for large components, capacity is limited to k.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Using size instead of min(k,size) when calculating total tunnel capacity.

special_cases.description: k = 1. Then each province can have at most one tunnel. Effectively, no province can have more than one tunnel, so the only way to connect multiple provinces is to merge them into a single province via roads. The minimal number of roads is max(0, (number of provinces) - 2), because if there are 2 provinces, we can connect them with one tunnel (using 2 capacities, each province provides 1). For 3 or more provinces, we need to reduce to at most 2 provinces via roads.
special_cases.test_values: n=5, m=0, k=1 => output 3 (since 5 components, reduce to 2 requires 3 roads).
special_cases.expected_behavior: Answer = max(0, components - 2) when k=1 (since each component capacity 1).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Thinking that with k=1, tunnels cannot be used at all, but they can connect exactly two provinces.

key_operations: DFS or BFS to find connected components
Greedy merge smallest sizes to meet condition
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to cap component capacity at k when computing total tunnel capacity
Assuming merging two components always increases or maintains total capacity (it can decrease if sum exceeds k)
Off-by-one in number of tunnels required (r-1) and capacity needed (2*(r-1))
Not handling the case where no tunnels are needed (already connected)
Using inefficient O(n^2) algorithm for large input

Since tree, maximum distinct edges you can traverse is all edges (n-1). But you need to plan a walk starting at root that can cover all edges? In a tree, you can only cover all edges if you can revisit nodes (Euler tour) but starting and ending at root? Actually you can traverse all edges exactly twice (back and forth) but you only pay once per edge. So maximum sum is sum of all edge costs. So for k>=n, answer is sum of all edge costs. But careful: each node can be visited at most k times, and root has initial visit. For a walk covering all edges, you might need to visit some nodes many times. But if k is large enough (≥ degree of nodes?) Actually to cover all edges, you need to traverse each edge once in each direction, so each node's visits equal its degree (except root may be visited start and end). So max visits needed is max degree. So if k >= max degree, answer is total sum. But constraint: k up to 1e5, n up to 1e5, degree can be up to n-1. So for star, degree of root is n-1, so if k < n-1, you cannot traverse all edges. So special case: large k but not necessarily covering all edges. The DP handles this.

special_cases.expected_behavior: output sum of all edge costs
special_cases.common_mistakes: not considering that large k allows more edges visited

special_cases.expected_behavior: answer is multiple of cost but same edge count logic
special_cases.common_mistakes: assuming costs matter only for sum, but greedy on costs works

common_pitfalls: State explosion if not careful; O(n*k) is too large; need to optimize using convexity or greedy? Actually solution uses DP with flow or matching? The problem is known as 'Heidi and the Turing Test' medium version; solution uses DP where dp[node][t] = max sum in subtree given node visited t times. implicit_constraints.description: The tree is rooted at vertex 1.
We can change the number of exactly one arbitrary vertex to 0 (or do nothing). Changing a vertex to 0 effectively removes it from GCD computation for any path that includes it.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Statement: 'can change the number in one arbitrary vertex to 0 or leave all vertices unchanged'

implicit_constraints.description: The number of distinct possible GCD values on a path from root is small (at most log2(max a_i) ≈ 18 because each time GCD either stays same or divides by a factor ≥2).
Recursion depth may be up to n (2e5), so iterative DFS or increasing recursion limit is needed.

special_cases.description: Root value is 1: Since 1 divides everything, the GCD of any path is 1 regardless of other numbers. However, setting a non-root vertex to 0 does not help because GCD of remaining numbers will still be 1 if any other number is 1? Actually GCD of numbers that include 1 is 1. So answer for every vertex is 1. But careful: if we set the vertex with value 1 to 0, then the path may no longer have 1, so GCD could be larger? But we can only set one vertex to 0. For a path that contains the root (value 1), if we set root to 0, then GCD becomes GCD of rest, which could be >1. However, the root itself: its path is just itself; if root is set to 0, beauty is 0. So maximum beauty for root is max(1,0)=1. For other vertices, we can set root to 0 to potentially increase GCD. So correct behavior: For any vertex whose path includes 1 (which includes all vertices since root is on every path), we can remove the 1 by setting root to 0, yielding a GCD of the remaining numbers. So answers could be greater than 1. But if the root is the only source of 1, removing it helps. Example: root=1, child=2, then child's path = [1,2]; remove root -> GCD(2)=2, so answer is 2. So this case requires careful handling. Many might incorrectly assume all answers are 1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming if root is 1, all answers are 1; not considering setting root to 0

special_cases.description: All numbers are the same: The GCD of any path without zero is that number. If we set a vertex to 0, the GCD might stay the same (if other numbers maintain GCD) or become larger? Actually GCD of same numbers is that number, and removing one might still be that number (if at least one remains). But if path has only one vertex (root), setting to 0 gives 0, so max is the number itself. So for each vertex, the maximum beauty is the common number.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Overthinking

special_cases.description: Large prime numbers: The GCD of a path is likely 1 unless all numbers share a common factor.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming GCD of path is always the minimum value, etc.

key_operations: Maintaining a set of possible GCDs for each node (with and without removing one vertex)
common_pitfalls: Recursion depth exceeding limit for n=200000 (use iterative DFS or set recursionlimit)
Not handling the case where we set the root to 0
Assuming the set of possible GCDs is large; but it's small (logarithmic) so using a set of integers is fine
Incorrectly updating the set when moving down the tree

implicit_constraints.description: n is even, so positions come in pairs (i, n-i+1). For each pair, the two characters must be different.
The string must have a permutation that is antipalindromic, meaning for each character, its frequency cannot exceed n/2 (since each pair needs distinct chars). But it is guaranteed to exist.
Maximum beauty is at most sum of all b_i, achieved when t = s exactly, but that may not be antipalindromic.

special_cases.description: When all b_i are equal (e.g., all 1), the problem reduces to checking if t can equal s while being antipalindromic, i.e., if s itself is antipalindromic. If not, some matches must be sacrificed, but because all b_i equal, any match gives same beauty. So the maximum beauty is the maximum number of positions that can keep original characters while satisfying antipalindrome condition. This is a combinatorial matching problem.
special_cases.test_values: n=8, s='abacabac', b_i all 1 -> output 8 (since s is antipalindromic?) Actually example 1: n=8, s=abacabac, b all 1, output 8, meaning s is antipalindromic? Check: s = a b a c a b a c, positions: 1 vs 8: a vs c? not equal, 2 vs 7: b vs a? not equal, 3 vs 6: a vs b? not equal, 4 vs 5: c vs a? not equal. So s is antipalindromic. So beauty = sum of all b_i = 8.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Solution must handle the case where many b_i are equal by using flow or matching to maximize count of matches.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming that maximizing matches is trivial or that greedy works; may incorrectly think that if all b_i are equal, any matching works, but need to satisfy antipalindrome constraint.

special_cases.description: When s is already antipalindromic, the maximum beauty is sum of all b_i (by taking t = s).
special_cases.test_values: Any s that is antipalindromic, e.g., n=2, s='ab', b_1=10, b_2=20 -> output 30.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Solution should correctly detect that t = s is valid and return total sum.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not considering that the identity permutation is always allowed if it satisfies constraints.

special_cases.description: When there are many duplicate characters, the matching becomes constrained. For example, if one character appears more than n/2 times, it's impossible to have an antipalindromic permutation, but input guarantees existence, so this case does not occur.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming no such guarantee and handling it incorrectly.

problem_type_analysis.sub_category: minimum cost flow (or maximum weight matching) on bipartite graph
key_operations: Construct bipartite graph with left side characters (by type) and right side positions (pairs), or more commonly, construct flow network where we match characters to positions with constraints that each position can receive at most one character, and each character type has capacity equal to its count, and for each pair (i, n-i+1), the two positions must have different characters.

Alternatively, model as assignment problem with constraints: we want to maximize sum over i of b_i * [t_i == s_i] subject to t being a permutation of s and for each i: t_i != t_{n-i+1}. This can be solved via min-cost max-flow where we have edges from source to character types, character types to positions, and positions to sink, with costs reflecting beauty if t_i == s_i (negative for max).
Use Hungarian algorithm with constraints? But n up to 100, flow works.
common_pitfalls: Misunderstanding the constraint: pairs (i, n-i+1) must have different letters, not just i != n-i+1.
Not handling the symmetry correctly; typical flow construction treats each pair as a unit that must receive two different characters.
Using integer overflow if b_i sum can be large (max sum = 100 * 100 = 10000, so safe).
Assuming greedy works (e.g., matching positions with highest b_i first) – not optimal due to constraints.

implicit_constraints.triggered_by: The reversal operation and the parity question

special_cases.common_mistakes: Incorrectly computing parity change by treating length 1 as odd (len*(len-1)/2 = 0, even, so no flip).

special_cases.description: Query where the reversed segment length is 2. Then len*(len-1)/2 = 1 (odd), so parity flips.

special_cases.expected_behavior: Output 'odd' after the query if previous was 'even'.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting to update the parity correctly.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming the permutation resets or not updating state.

special_cases.common_mistakes: assuming any triple exists

special_cases.common_mistakes: forgetting ordering condition a ≤ b ≤ c

special_cases.description: n = 6: only valid triple is (3,5,6) as per example.

key_operations: check c = a xor b <= n and a+b>c
common_pitfalls: forgetting to ensure a ≤ b ≤ c
forgetting triangle inequality
assuming a xor b automatically satisfies c ≥ b (it doesn't always)

input_format.description: First line contains three integers n, l, r. Second line contains n integers a_i. Third line contains n integers b_i.

output_format.description: Print a single integer, the maximum possible convenience.

implicit_constraints.description: The total height of all boxes is at most 10000, which bounds the cumulative sums for DP.
Boxes can be reordered, so the order is a permutation. Important boxes count only if their bottom edge falls in [l, r].
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem description of reordering and convenience definition

boundary_conditions.condition: Minimum and maximum number of boxes

special_cases.description: All boxes are important
special_cases.expected_behavior: Maximum convenience is number of boxes whose bottom edge (cumulative sum) falls in [l, r]. Since order matters, we need to arrange boxes to maximize this count. Typically, you want to place as many important boxes with cumulative sum in interval as possible.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming that simply counting all important boxes works; need to consider ordering and cumulative sums.

special_cases.description: All boxes are unimportant
special_cases.common_mistakes: None.

special_cases.description: l = 0 and r = 0
special_cases.expected_behavior: Only the bottom edge at height 0 counts, so only the first box in the order (if important) can contribute. Maximum convenience is 1 if there is at least one important box, else 0.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming all boxes with bottom edge 0 count, but only one box can have bottom edge 0.

special_cases.description: Total height less than l
special_cases.expected_behavior: No box can have bottom edge in [l, r] because the maximum bottom edge is total height < l. Convenience is 0.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming some box might still count if l is small; but l > total height means no interval.

special_cases.expected_behavior: Bottom edge of the only box is 0. If b1=1 and 0 in [l,r] then convenience=1 else 0.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Forgetting that bottom edge is 0 for the first box.

key_operations: Sort boxes by importance? Actually important and unimportant boxes need different treatment.
DP over total height to maximize count of important boxes with bottom in [l, r]
Consider placing important boxes at positions where cumulative sum falls in interval
common_pitfalls: Not accounting that order is arbitrary, so we can choose which important boxes are placed at which cumulative sums.
Assuming that we can only place important boxes consecutively; we can mix unimportant boxes anywhere.
Not handling the case where l > total height.
Complexity: O(n * total_height) with total_height <= 10000, but n up to 10000, need efficient DP.

input_format.description: Three lines: first line contains integer n, second line contains n integers (a permutation of 1..n), third line contains a binary string of length n-1 indicating allowed swaps.

output_format.description: Print YES if the array can be sorted using allowed adjacent swaps, otherwise NO.

explicit.description: Number of elements in the array.
Each element is an integer from 1 to n (permutation), but constraint given as 1 ≤ a_i ≤ 200000.

implicit_constraints.description: The array a is a permutation of integers from 1 to n: each integer appears exactly once.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Statement: Each integer from 1 to n appears exactly once.

implicit_constraints.description: For each i where swaps[i]=='0' (barrier), the prefix up to i must contain exactly the numbers 1..i, i.e., the maximum of a[1..i] must equal i.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: The condition for sortability: elements cannot cross barriers, so each segment between barriers must contain the correct numbers.

boundary_conditions.condition: Extreme cases: no swaps allowed or all swaps allowed.

special_cases.description: Array already sorted: always YES.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Thinking that swaps are needed even when already sorted.

special_cases.description: All swaps allowed (string of all '1'): always YES, as any permutation can be sorted by bubble sort.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not realizing that unrestricted adjacent swaps allow full sorting.

special_cases.description: No swaps allowed (string of all '0'): only YES if array already sorted; otherwise NO.
special_cases.expected_behavior: YES only if a is sorted ascending.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming you can still swap somehow.

special_cases.description: Barrier at position i but prefix max > i: impossible.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output NO because prefix max at i=1 is 2 > 1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not checking prefix maximum at barriers.

key_operations: Compute prefix maximum of the array.
Check at each barrier (swaps[i]=='0') that prefix_max[i] equals i.
common_pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when indexing the swap string (length n-1).
Assuming that only adjacent swaps at one position are allowed, but they can be chained.
Not realizing that barriers partition the array into independent segments.

Not handling p=1 case where phi(p) is 1 and counting function simplifies.

input_format.description: The first line contains two integers n and k.

implicit_constraints.description: The number of terms k must be at least the popcount of n (number of 1 bits in binary representation), otherwise impossible.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Each term is a power of two, and the sum of popcount(n) terms can only be increased by splitting, never decreased.

implicit_constraints.description: The maximum exponent in the sequence must be minimized; achieved by repeatedly splitting the largest exponent until the sequence length is k.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Requirement of smallest possible y (maximum exponent).

implicit_constraints.description: The lexicographically largest sequence among those with minimized max exponent is obtained by sorting the multiset of exponents in descending order.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Definition of lexicographic order: larger earlier element is better.

boundary_conditions.condition: minimum, small, maximum, near max power of two

special_cases.description: n=1, k=2: only possible sequence is -1 -1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Trying to use exponent 0 and negative fractions incorrectly.

special_cases.description: n=13, k=2: impossible because popcount(13)=3 > 2.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Trying to combine exponents into two terms by using negative exponents, but sum would not be 13.

special_cases.description: n=23, k=5: given sample output.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not achieving minimal max exponent (should be 3) or lexicographically largest (should start with 3).

special_cases.description: n is a power of two with large k, e.g., n=8, k=5: many splits needed.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output Yes and a sequence with exponents descending, e.g., 1 1 1 0 0
special_cases.common_mistakes: Splitting in wrong order leading to suboptimal lexicographic order.

common_pitfalls: Not checking feasibility: if k < popcount(n), output No.
Incorrect splitting order leading to suboptimal maximum exponent.
Not sorting descending for lexicographic order.

input_format.description: First line contains integers n and m. Then m lines each contain two integers u and v describing a road.

output_format.description: Single integer r, the minimum number of roads to build, or -1 if impossible.

implicit_constraints.description: Graph may have self-loops and multiple edges, but they do not affect connectivity; they can be ignored when finding component sizes.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement allows self-loops and multiple roads.

implicit_constraints.description: The sum of all component sizes is exactly n.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Each island belongs to exactly one component.

implicit_constraints.description: Only lucky numbers (digits 4 and 7) up to n matter; there are O(log n) such numbers.
The answer is -1 if no subset of component sizes sums to a lucky number.

boundary_conditions.condition: min (one component of size n) and max (each island separate)

special_cases.description: Already a lucky region: there exists a component with size 4 or 7 etc.
special_cases.test_values: n=4, m=0 (but m>=1, so can't have zero; but a component of size 4 exists, e.g., 4 islands connected).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming at least one road needed even if lucky region exists.

special_cases.description: Only one island (n=1): component size 1, not lucky. Cannot build roads between different regions. Output -1.
special_cases.test_values: n=1, m=1 (road can be self-loop or to itself).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Thinking that building a road to itself creates a lucky region? It doesn't change size.

special_cases.description: All islands isolated (each size 1): need to merge many components to get lucky sum. Minimum k such that sum of k ones is lucky. The smallest lucky number >1 is 4, so answer = 3.
special_cases.test_values: n=4, m=0? But m>=1, so if m=1 with self-loop? Actually if m=0 not allowed; but we can have m=1 connecting two islands, then components: one of size 2, two of size 1. Need to get lucky sum 4, so merge all three components: 2+1+1=4, roads=2. Or other.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not considering that merging more than two components is allowed.

special_cases.description: No lucky sum reachable: e.g., n=5 with components sizes 2 and 3. Possible sums: 2,3,5. 5 is not lucky (lucky numbers: 4,7,...). So output -1.
special_cases.test_values: n=5, edges forming two components of sizes 2 and 3.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming if total n is lucky then answer is 0? Wrong, need a single lucky region; merging all gives 5, not lucky.

key_operations: Use DSU to find connected components and their sizes.
Compress component sizes by frequency (count of each size).
Solve bounded knapsack (min items to achieve sum) using binary splitting or monotone queue.
Check all lucky numbers up to n for minimum items, then answer = min_items - 1.
If no lucky sum reachable, output -1.
common_pitfalls: Using naive DP O(n * number_of_components) leads to TLE (10^10).
Forgetting to handle self-loops and multiple edges in DSU.
Assuming that answer is always 0 if total islands is lucky (need a single component).
Not considering that merging k components needs k-1 roads.
Overlooking that we can merge any subset, not necessarily all components.

special_cases.expected_behavior: Use special handling for ratio 1, e.g., sum = first_term * ((n+1)/k) modulo M
special_cases.common_mistakes: Applying geometric series formula with division by (1 - ratio) without checking if ratio is 1

input_format.description: The first line contains an integer n (number of tasks). Then n lines follow. Each line starts with an integer t (type). If t=1, an integer u follows. If t=2, three integers x, k, s follow.

output_format.description: For each type 2 task, output a single integer: the desired number or -1.

implicit_constraints.description: The condition k | gcd(x, a_i) implies both x and a_i must be multiples of k. Therefore, if k does not divide x, no number can satisfy the condition, and the answer is -1.
Values are positive integers; the array initially empty.
For queries with k=1, the divisibility condition always holds (since 1 divides any number), so the problem reduces to finding a number ≤ s that maximizes XOR with x.
The maximum possible XOR value is bounded by the highest bit of the maximum number (e.g., 2^17 - 1 for numbers up to 10^5).

boundary_conditions.condition: min and max x in query

special_cases.description: No number satisfies the condition (e.g., array empty, or no multiple of k ≤ s, or x not divisible by k). Output -1.
special_cases.test_values: any query where no valid a_i exists
special_cases.common_mistakes: forgetting to check if k divides x first

special_cases.description: Multiple numbers satisfy and produce the same maximum XOR value. The problem expects any such number.
special_cases.test_values: e.g., array [3,5], query (x=6, k=1, s=5) -> both 3 and 5 yield XOR=7? Actually 6 XOR 3 = 5, 6 XOR 5 = 3, so max is 5. But if multiple yield same, e.g., array [1,3], query (x=2, k=1, s=3): 2 XOR 1 = 3, 2 XOR 3 = 1, max=3, output 1 or 3? But 1 gives XOR=3? Actually 2 XOR 1 = 3, 2 XOR 3 = 1, so max XOR is 3 from 1. So only one. Example: array [5,6], query (x=3, k=1, s=6): 3 XOR 5 = 6, 3 XOR 6 = 5, both yield 6? No, 3 XOR 5 = 6, 3 XOR 6 = 5, 6 > 5. So unique. To get equal, e.g., array [0,3] but 0 not allowed. Actually numbers positive. So equal XOR rarely. But if it happens, any is acceptable.
special_cases.expected_behavior: output any valid number that maximizes XOR
special_cases.common_mistakes: assuming a specific order or returning -1 when multiple exist

special_cases.description: Query when k is large (e.g., 100000) and s is small (e.g., 1): only number 1 can satisfy if 1 is present and divisible by 100000? Actually 1 is not divisible by 100000. So answer -1 unless multiple of k is present.
special_cases.test_values: k=100000, s=1, x=100000 (divisible by k), array contains 100000? But s=1; 100000 > s so not valid. So answer -1.
special_cases.expected_behavior: correctly iterate only over multiples of k ≤ s
special_cases.common_mistakes: iterating over all numbers instead of only multiples

key_operations: query for number satisfying divisibility and range constraint maximizing XOR
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to handle the case where k does not divide x; immediate -1
Not using a data structure that efficiently enforces the ≤ s constraint (e.g., storing minimum value in trie nodes)
Inefficiently iterating over all values for each query instead of using a trie

Seat width in centimeters; all w_i are distinct.

The number of extroverts equals the number of introverts, each equal to n.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming extrovert needs a different row, but only one row exists.

special_cases.description: When the introverts' choices are in increasing order of widths and extroverts appear later, the algorithm should correctly manage the heap transitions.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Introverts choose rows with smallest widths: row1 (width1) then row2 (width2); then extroverts choose rows with largest width among those with one seat: first extrovert chooses row2, second chooses row1. Output: '1 2 2 1'.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Mixing up the heap order or forgetting to remove from min-heap after introvert.

key_operations: Maintain a min-heap of empty rows (keyed by width) for introverts.

Not handling the fact that widths are distinct, so heaps can be keyed by width directly.
Forgetting that rows are 1-indexed and need to store row index alongside width.
Not ensuring that extrovert always finds a row (guaranteed by problem).

Assuming that any subtree with even size can be removed; but the complement must also be even, which holds if n is even.

explicit.description: x-coordinate of initial position, 0 <= x <= a
y-coordinate of initial position, 0 <= y <= b

implicit_constraints.description: vx and vy cannot both be zero (ball must move).
The initial position (x,y) is not a pocket, i.e., (x,y) not in {(0,0), (a,0), (0,b), (a,b)}.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Problem statement: initially not in a pocket

implicit_constraints.description: The direction of movement must be axis-aligned or at 45 degrees, i.e., either vx=0, vy=0, or |vx|=|vy|. This follows from the physics of the problem.
Reflections are perfect: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and speed magnitude remains constant.

The ball's path is periodic and deterministic. It will eventually fall into a pocket if and only if there exist integers k,l such that (x + t*vx) mod (2a) equals 0 or a, and (y + t*vy) mod (2b) equals 0 or b for some t.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Geometry of reflections and pocket positions

boundary_conditions.condition: boundaries of x relative to a
boundaries of y relative to b

special_cases.description: Ball moves vertically (vx=0) but not along left or right side. Similar infinite loop.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Same as above.

special_cases.description: Ball starts exactly on a side but not at a corner, and moves along that side toward the corner. It will fall into that corner pocket.
special_cases.test_values: e.g., vy=0, y=0, vx>0 (bottom side, moving right) -> pocket (a,0); or vx=0, x=0, vy>0 -> pocket (0,b)
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not handling this case because it's along a side, but it's similar to the general case.

special_cases.description: Diagonal movement where the ball never aligns with a corner due to parity or gcd conditions.
special_cases.test_values: e.g., a=4, b=3, start (2,2), vx=-1, vy=1 (first sample) -> pocket (0,0). Another: a=4, b=4, start (2,0), vx=1, vy=1 -> the ball might never hit a corner? Actually sample 2 gives -1. So such cases test infinite diagonal paths.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Output -1 if never hits pocket, else pocket coordinates.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming diagonal always hits a pocket; not using number theory to check.

special_cases.description: Ball starts at a corner? Not allowed, but just in case.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Not considered as per problem statement (guaranteed not in pocket).
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not checking condition initially.

key_operations: Reflect the table to transform the problem into a straight line in an infinite grid
Use extended Euclidean algorithm to find if the line passes through a lattice point (k*a, l*b)
Handle sign and parity to determine which pocket

input_format.description: A single integer n representing the initial number of candies.

output_format.description: Output a single integer k — the minimal amount of candies Vasya should eat each morning.

explicit.description: initial amount of candies in the box (1 ≤ n ≤ 1e18)

implicit_constraints.description: k must be at least 1 and at most n
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: Vasya eats k candies each morning, so k cannot exceed the initial amount n and must be positive integer.

implicit_constraints.description: Petya eats floor of remaining/10 candies, so for n < 10, Petya never eats.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: The process description: if less than 10 candies, Petya takes none.

implicit_constraints.description: Vasya's total candies eaten is a non-decreasing function of k, enabling binary search.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: As k increases, Vasya eats more per day, so total can only increase or stay same.

implicit_constraints.description: Use 64-bit integers (e.g., long long) as n can be up to 1e18.

boundary_conditions.condition: min, small values around threshold where Petya starts eating, max

special_cases.description: When n is small (n < 10), Petya never eats any candies, so Vasya will eventually eat all candies regardless of k. Therefore the minimal k is 1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Assuming k must be larger for n=1 or n=2, or not considering that process continues until box empty.

special_cases.description: When n is large, the answer is typically found via binary search with simulation. Common mistake is to simulate inefficiently or not handle overflow.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Binary search with O(log n) simulation per check, runs within time.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Not using 64-bit integers, infinite loop in simulation if not careful, incorrect condition for Vasya's total >= ceil(n/2).

key_operations: Binary search on k from 1 to n
Simulate days: subtract k, then subtract floor(remaining/10)
common_pitfalls: Off-by-one in binary search boundaries
Incorrect simulation of Petya's eating (floor division)
Using int (32-bit) leads to overflow
Forgetting to include Vasya's last meal when remaining < k

input_format.description: First line contains two integers n and m. Then m lines each contain three integers ai, bi, wi denoting an edge from ai to bi with weight wi.

output_format.description: Print a single integer representing the maximum number of edges in the path.

implicit_constraints.description: Selected edges must form a subsequence of the input edges in order, i.e., the sequence of selected edge indices must be strictly increasing.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: phrase 'these edges come in the order of input' in problem description

implicit_constraints.description: Weights along the path must be strictly increasing, so no two edges with the same weight can be used consecutively.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: phrase 'weights of the edges are in strictly increasing order'

implicit_constraints.description: Graph may contain multiple edges and self-loops, which is allowed.
Graph is directed but can be disconnected; path can revisit vertices.
Solution must be efficient, typically O(m log W) or O(m log m) due to constraints up to 1e5.
implicit_constraints.triggered_by: max constraints of n and m (100000)

boundary_conditions.condition: minimum and maximum number of vertices
minimum and maximum number of edges
minimum and maximum starting vertex (also at most n)
minimum and maximum ending vertex (also at most n)

special_cases.expected_behavior: The path can consist of this single edge, answer=1.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Overlooking that self-loops are allowed and can be used.

special_cases.description: Multiple edges with same weight between same vertices: only one can be used.
special_cases.expected_behavior: Answer=1, since two edges with same weight cannot be consecutive.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Incorrectly allowing both because of same weight.

special_cases.common_mistakes: Sorting by weight and ignoring input order could give answer=2.

special_cases.description: All edges have same weight: no two edges can be used in a path.
special_cases.common_mistakes: Using dynamic programming that allows equal weights.

input_format.description: The only line contains two integer numbers n and H

output_format.description: Print the minimum number of spots you can occupy

implicit_constraints.description: n and H up to 10^18 require O(log n) or O(sqrt(n)) time complexity; O(n) is impossible
The height difference constraint |hi - hi+1| <= 1 forces the shape to be a unimodal 'mountain' (non-decreasing then non-increasing) possibly with a flat plateau
All sand must be used exactly; the sum of heights equals n
The first pillar height must be <= H, so the shape cannot start higher than H
The answer is the minimal number of occupied spots (positive heights); spots beyond are zero

special_cases.description: When n <= H, the answer is 1 because we can put all sand in the first pillar without exceeding the fence height
special_cases.common_mistakes: not handling this early exit; trying to construct longer shape unnecessarily

special_cases.description: When H is very large compared to n, the answer is 1 (same as above). However, if H is large but n is also large, the optimal shape may start with a high pillar and then descend; the check function must handle descending sequences correctly
special_cases.expected_behavior: output 1 if n<=H, else compute minimal spots
special_cases.common_mistakes: assuming shape must always increase first; not considering descending-only shape

special_cases.description: When n is very large (e.g., 10^18) and H is small (e.g., 1), the answer is about 2*sqrt(n) and the solution must handle large integers without overflow
special_cases.expected_behavior: output a large number around 2*10^9 (actually, with H=1, the optimal shape can start at 1, go up, then down; the maximal sum for k spots is roughly (k^2+2k)/4 for even k? need precise. But anyway, the answer should be computed correctly.
special_cases.common_mistakes: integer overflow in languages like C++ when computing sums; using Python avoids this but still careful with large numbers

key_operations: binary search on number of spots k
compute maximum possible sand that can be placed in k spots given H
common_pitfalls: Overflow in intermediate calculations (especially in C++)
Incorrect handling of plateau or descending shapes
Off-by-one errors in binary search or sum formulas
Assuming the shape is always symmetric (it may be descending if H is large)
